description: The Sirens promise absolute knowledge. Odysseus is the only mortal who hears their song and lives, thanks to a trick that became a model of self-control.

hero.hook: Their song promises all knowledge. Everyone who listens dies. Odysseus wants to hear it and stay alive.

blocks.text: In Book Twelve of the **Odyssey**, Odysseus has to sail past the **[[Sirens]]**. Their voices are so beautiful that they cancel the will. Sailors who come close run aground and die.

This is not just a sea adventure. It is a duel between the thirst for knowledge and the danger of giving in. Thanks to his [[Metis]], his cunning intelligence, Odysseus becomes the only mortal to taste that forbidden pleasure and keep his life.
In **Homer**, the Sirens are not fish-women. They are half woman, half bird. Their island is littered with the bones of sailors. The beauty of the song clashes with the horror of the shore.

blocks.caption: The island of the Sirens: an irresistible melody, a deadly shore

blocks.text: Greek cities often carved Sirens onto tombs. They were seen as muses of the afterlife, escorting the souls of the dead.

Their trap is not only sensual. They promise **absolute knowledge**: everything that happened in the [[Trojan War]], everything that happens on earth. For Odysseus, curious above all, this is the supreme temptation, more dangerous than any monster to beat.
The sorceress **Circe** has warned him. Odysseus prepares an exact plan. He plugs his crew's ears with **beeswax**. They must hear nothing. He wants to listen.

blocks.caption: Odysseus tied to the mast, the only man to hear the Sirens' song

blocks.text: He has himself **tied to the mast**. The order is clear: if he begs to be freed, the ropes must be pulled tighter. When the song rises, Odysseus loses his calm and shouts to be released. His men, deaf and loyal to the plan, obey only the rational Odysseus of an hour before, not the spellbound Odysseus of the moment. The ship sails on.

sections.title: The wax, the mast, and the plan

blocks.text: The scene illustrates what social scientists call [[Precommitment]]. You know you will be weak in front of a temptation. So you cut down your own options before you get there.
In 1990, NASA and ESA named a probe **Ulysses**. Like the hero, it left the known routes to explore the poles of the Sun.

The Nobel-winning economist **Richard Thaler** leans on this image. People are not always rational. They need a [[Nudge]], a “gentle push,” or rules that protect them from themselves: an automatic transfer into savings, an app that blocks social media. Like Odysseus, we tie ourselves to the mast against modern sirens.

sections.title: Tying yourself down before the temptation

blocks.text: In the **Middle Ages**, the picture changed. The bird-woman became a fish-woman. The Church read the Sirens as symbols of lust. Odysseus' mast was sometimes compared to the cross, a shield against temptation.

In Homer, though, the stake was not desire of the flesh but knowledge. Odysseus is neither a saint nor a simple adventurer. He is a man who uses his mind to steer between the hunger for the absolute and the need to stay alive.
Odysseus survives the song of the [[Sirens]] through [[Precommitment]]: tied to the mast, he listens, while his men, ears plugged with wax, hold the course.

subtitle: Listening without dying
title: Odysseus and the Sirens
